noteBlocks.lede: A magnet's pull reaches out into the space around it: its magnetic field. A compass can map that field, and a coil carrying a current makes the same field, one you can switch on and off. That is an electromagnet, and you will learn exactly what makes it stronger.
can: Draw and read the field lines of a bar magnet and of a coil
Find a coil's poles from its current, and its current from its poles
Name the three ways to make an electromagnet stronger or weaker

noteBlocks.caption: Field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole; they crowd together where the field is strongest.

noteBlocks.md: Field lines show the field's shape and direction. Outside the magnet they run **from the north pole to the south pole**, with an arrow on every line. They never cross, and crowd **closest near the poles**, where the field is strongest. A **plotting compass** points its north end along a line, the way of the arrow.

Read the bar magnet in the figure:
**Which end do the lines leave?** The north end; they enter the south end.
**Which way do the needles point?** Along the lines, from north round to south.

noteBlocks.prompt: A pupil draws the field lines curving over the top of a bar magnet and must add the arrows. Which way should they point?
options: from the north pole to the south pole
from the south pole to the north pole
away from both poles
noteBlocks.answer: from the north pole to the south pole
noteBlocks.explain: Look at the arrows round the bar magnet: every line leaves the north end, curves round and goes into the south end, and each compass needle points the same way. So outside the magnet the field runs from the north pole to the south pole.

noteBlocks.caption: Mark where the needle points, move the compass on, and repeat: the dots make one field line.

noteBlocks.md: A plotting compass is a tiny magnet: its needle lines up along the field line it sits on, its north end pointing the way of the arrow. Stepping it along from pole to pole traces one line. Iron filings show the shape quickly, but not the direction: only a compass gives that.

Worked, for the compasses in the figure:
1. Set the first compass beside the north pole and mark a dot where its north end points.
2. Move the compass on so its tail sits on that dot, and mark again.
3. Carry on to the south pole, then join the dots and add the arrow.

noteBlocks.prompt: Compasses are placed one after another along a field line that runs from a bar magnet's north pole over to its south pole. Which way does each needle's north end point?
options: along the line, on towards the south pole
along the line, back towards the north pole
straight at the middle of the magnet
noteBlocks.answer: along the line, on towards the south pole
noteBlocks.explain: Look at the five compasses in the picture: each needle lies along the dashed line, and its filled north end points on towards the south pole, because the field runs from north to south outside the magnet. That is why each new dot is marked where the north end points. The answer is along the line, on towards the south pole.

noteBlocks.md: A current in a coil makes a magnetic field. Outside, it is **shaped like a bar magnet's**, with a north and a south end; inside, the lines are **straight and parallel**, running from south to north. The current's direction decides which end is north.

noteBlocks.caption: Look at one end: current going anticlockwise makes it a north pole; clockwise makes it a south pole.

noteBlocks.md: To find the poles, look at one end and follow the current round: **anticlockwise** makes it a **north** pole, **clockwise** a **south** pole. The other end is the opposite pole.

Worked, for the two ends in the figure:
1. Left circle: the current goes anticlockwise, so that end is a north pole.
2. Right circle: the current goes clockwise, so that end is a south pole.

noteBlocks.prompt: Looking straight at one end of a coil, the current flows clockwise. Which pole is that end?
options: a south pole
a north pole
no pole: only bar magnets have poles
noteBlocks.explain: Use the end rule from the two circles: anticlockwise makes a north pole and clockwise makes a south pole. A coil carrying a current has poles just as a bar magnet does. So a clockwise current makes this end a south pole.

noteBlocks.md: Turn the cell round and the current flows the other way through the coil. The field keeps exactly the same shape, but **every arrow reverses**, so the **north and south poles swap ends**. The field is no stronger and no weaker: the current's size has not changed, only its direction.

Compare the two coils in the figure:
1. As wired: north is at the left end.
2. Cell turned round: every arrow reverses, and north is now at the right end.

options: the north and south poles swap ends
the field becomes stronger
the field disappears
noteBlocks.answer: the north and south poles swap ends
noteBlocks.explain: Compare the two coils in the picture: with the cell turned round, each field arrow points the other way, so the pole that was on the left is now on the right. The same current flows, so the strength is unchanged. The answer is that the poles swap ends.

noteBlocks.md: The end rule works backwards too. Find the north end (the field lines leave it), look at the coil from an end, and choose the current that makes that pole: anticlockwise for north, clockwise for south. Inside the coil the field runs **from south to north**, so each line is a closed loop.

Worked from the right-hand end in the figure:
1. The field lines enter the right end, so it is a south pole.
2. From that end, a south pole needs the current clockwise.
3. From there the front of the coil is on your left, where clockwise runs upwards: at X the current flows up.

it cannot be told from the field lines
noteBlocks.explain: Field lines leave a north pole, so the right-hand end is north. The end rule, read backwards as in the worked lines: seen from a north pole, the current runs anticlockwise. The answer is anticlockwise.

noteBlocks.caption: Three changes make an electromagnet stronger: more current, more turns and a soft iron core.

noteBlocks.md: A coil with a core, used as a switchable magnet, is an **electromagnet**. Three changes make it stronger: **more current**, **more turns** of wire, and a **soft iron core**. The opposites make it weaker: less current, fewer turns, or taking the core out.

noteBlocks.title: Why soft iron
noteBlocks.md: Soft iron is strongly magnetised while the current flows and loses its magnetism when it stops, so the electromagnet can be switched off: that is how a scrapyard crane drops its load.

**The nails investigation.** Booklet B (Summer 2021) changed the current and counted the iron nails held:
**Changed.** The current.
**Measured.** The nails held, twice at each current, then averaged.
**Kept the same.** The turns and the core.

Worked first on a coil lifting paper clips as its core is changed:
**What is changed on purpose?** The core: independent.
**What is counted each time?** The paper clips: dependent.

noteBlocks.prompt: A pupil changes the current through an electromagnet and counts the iron nails it holds. What is the dependent variable?

the current
the number of turns
noteBlocks.explain: The dependent variable is the one measured each time, as in the investigation above: the number of nails held. The current is the one changed on purpose, so it is the independent variable, and the turns are kept the same. The answer is the number of nails held.

prompts.answer: From the north pole to the south pole.

prompts.prompt: Name three ways to make an electromagnet stronger.
prompts.answer: More current, more turns on the coil, and a soft iron core.

prompts.prompt: What happens to a coil's poles when its current is reversed?
prompts.answer: They swap ends: the field keeps its shape but every arrow reverses.

prompts.prompt: What instrument shows the direction of a magnetic field?
Seen from one end of a coil, the current runs anticlockwise. Which pole is that end?
prompts.answer: A north pole; clockwise would make it a south pole.
